name: Snowdonia & North Wales
tagline: Wales's mountainous heart: a national park of jagged peaks and slate-grey lakes, ringed by castles built to hold the country down and a coastline that rewards anyone who reaches it.
highlight: Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) at sunrise, Wales's highest peak and the reason the whole national park carries its old English name.
shortDescription: A mountainous national park in north Wales, built around Yr Wyddfa's peak, ringed by medieval castles and slate heritage towns, with a dramatic coastline nearby.
metaDescription: A Snowdonia and North Wales travel guide: Yr Wyddfa, Conwy Castle, the Llanberis slate landscape, when to go and a practical multi-day itinerary.
knownFor: Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon), castles, slate heritage, Welsh coastline

image.file: File:Yr Wyddfa towards Llyn Llydaw Crib Goch 2019 01.jpg
image.alt: The ridge and lake of Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon), seen from near its summit

intro: Snowdonia — Eryri in Welsh, the name now officially used alongside the English one — is a national park built around Yr Wyddfa, Wales's highest mountain at 1,085 metres, and the jagged, glacier-carved range surrounding it. It is mountainous in a way little else in England or Wales quite matches, with real scrambling routes, sharp ridgelines and weather that turns fast.

The park sits within a wider region shaped by two very different forces: Edward I's 13th-century castle-building campaign, which left Conwy and Caernarfon among the most complete medieval fortresses in Europe, and the 19th-century slate industry, which built entire towns like Blaenau Ffestiniog and Llanberis around quarrying the mountains themselves.

The coastline nearby is an underrated part of the trip — the Llŷn Peninsula and Anglesey offer beaches and cliff walks that feel a world away from the mountains just inland, and the combination of the two in one compact region is a large part of what makes North Wales worth the distance from England's south.

whyVisit.intro: Snowdonia's case is that nowhere else in England or Wales packs genuine mountain scrambling, complete medieval castles and a dramatic coastline into one manageable region.

points.title: The mountains are serious
points.text: Yr Wyddfa and its neighbouring ridges offer real scrambling and exposed terrain, a different order of challenge from most English hill walking.

points.title: The castles are among Europe's best preserved
points.text: Conwy and Caernarfon, both UNESCO-listed, survive largely intact — a rare thing for medieval fortresses this old.

points.title: The slate heritage is a story found nowhere else
points.text: Entire mountainsides and towns were shaped by an industry that literally quarried the landscape, now preserved rather than erased.

points.title: The coastline is a genuine bonus
points.text: Anglesey and the Llŷn Peninsula add beaches and sea cliffs that most mountain-focused visitors don't expect to find so close by.

points.title: Welsh culture and language are present
points.text: Welsh is widely spoken as a first language here, giving the region a distinct cultural identity rather than feeling like an extension of England.

attractionsIntro: A mix of mountain, castle and heritage sights that together capture the different sides of this region.

attractions.name: Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon)

image.file: File:Train on the Snowdon Mountain Railway - geograph.org.uk - 5550136.jpg
image.alt: A train on the Snowdon Mountain Railway climbing Yr Wyddfa

attractions.text: Wales's highest peak at 1,085 metres, reachable by several walking routes or the Snowdon Mountain Railway, with views stretching to Ireland on a clear day.
attractions.tip: The Llanberis Path is the longest but gentlest route; the Pyg Track and Miners' Track are more scenic but steeper.

attractions.name: Conwy Castle

image.alt: The towers and walls of Conwy Castle

attractions.text: A UNESCO World Heritage castle built by Edward I in the 1280s, its eight towers and largely intact walls forming one of the most complete medieval fortresses in Britain.
attractions.tip: Walk the town walls, also largely intact, for a free and dramatic view over the castle and estuary.

attractions.name: Caernarfon Castle

image.alt: Caernarfon Castle's imposing walls and towers

attractions.text: Another Edward I fortress, built partly to evoke Constantinople's walls and used for the investiture of the Prince of Wales, among the most imposing castles in Britain.
attractions.tip: Climb the towers for views over the Menai Strait toward Anglesey.

attractions.name: Llanberis and the Slate Landscape

image.file: File:Dinorwig Slate Quarry from Llanberis - geograph.org.uk - 6263827.jpg
image.alt: The terraced slate quarry above Llanberis

attractions.text: A former slate-quarrying town at the foot of Snowdon, now a UNESCO World Heritage site telling the story of the industry that shaped the region's mountains and towns.
attractions.tip: The National Slate Museum, in a former quarry workshop, is free to enter and well presented.

attractions.name: Portmeirion

image.alt: The colourful Italianate buildings of Portmeirion village

attractions.text: An eccentric, brightly coloured Italianate village built by architect Clough Williams-Ellis over five decades, unlike anywhere else in Wales.
attractions.tip: Famous as the filming location for the 1960s TV series The Prisoner, still celebrated by an annual fan festival.

attractions.name: The Llŷn Peninsula and Anglesey

image.file: File:South Stack Lighthouse on the Edge of the Cliffs – Anglesey, Wales.jpg
image.alt: South Stack Lighthouse perched on cliffs off Anglesey

attractions.text: A quieter coastal side to the region, with beaches, cliff walks and the pilgrimage island of Bardsey off the Llŷn, and South Stack's cliffs on Anglesey.
attractions.tip: Both reward at least a full day — they are different in character from the mountainous interior.

thingsToDoIntro: Beyond the headline sights, this region rewards a mix of mountain activity and slower coastal and heritage time.

thingsToDo.title: Hike or ride Yr Wyddfa

image.file: File:Walkers on the Pyg-Miners' Track on Snowdon - geograph.org.uk - 3449005.jpg
image.alt: Walkers on the Pyg Track heading up Yr Wyddfa

thingsToDo.text: Reaching the summit on foot, or by the historic Snowdon Mountain Railway for those not up for the climb, is the region's central experience.
thingsToDo.tip: Book the railway well ahead in summer — it sells out, and walking remains free and available regardless of ticket availability.

thingsToDo.title: Ride the Snowdonia zip lines and underground trampolines
thingsToDo.text: Former slate quarries near Llanberis and Blaenau Ffestiniog have been repurposed into inventive attractions — Europe's fastest zip line and vast underground trampoline networks.
thingsToDo.tip: Both require advance booking and are hugely popular in school holidays.

thingsToDo.title: Walk the Conwy or Caernarfon town walls

image.alt: Conwy's medieval town walls and a gate tower

thingsToDo.text: Both towns retain substantial medieval walls, walkable for free and giving excellent views over the castles and surrounding water.
thingsToDo.tip: Conwy's walls form a more complete circuit than Caernarfon's — allow about an hour to walk the full loop.

thingsToDo.title: Visit a slate cavern tour

image.alt: The underground slate caverns at Llechwedd

thingsToDo.text: Former working slate mines, particularly around Blaenau Ffestiniog, now offer underground tours giving a genuine sense of the industry's scale and conditions.
thingsToDo.tip: Bring a jacket — the caverns stay cool year-round regardless of the weather outside.

thingsToDo.title: Explore the Llŷn Peninsula's beaches

image.file: File:Porth Oer....Whistling Sands, Llyn Peninsula, Wales - geograph.org.uk - 4976829.jpg
image.alt: The sandy cove of Porth Oer (Whistling Sands) on the Llŷn Peninsula

thingsToDo.text: A quieter, more remote coastline than much of Wales, with beaches like Porth Oer (Whistling Sands) and dramatic cliff walks around Aberdaron.
thingsToDo.tip: The peninsula's far end feels remote — allow more driving time than distances alone suggest.

thingsToDo.title: Ride a heritage railway

image.file: File:Blaenau Ffestiniog - steam train entering station - geograph.org.uk - 6010435.jpg
image.alt: A heritage steam train entering Blaenau Ffestiniog station

thingsToDo.text: North Wales has a strong network of narrow-gauge heritage railways, including the Ffestiniog and Welsh Highland lines through dramatic mountain scenery.
thingsToDo.tip: The Ffestiniog Railway is one of the oldest surviving railway companies in the world, dating to 1832.

foodIntro: Welsh food leans on hearty mountain and coastal traditions, with a few distinctive national dishes.

foods.name: Welsh rarebit

image.file: File:T@ Welsh Rarebit - T @ The Dials 2023-05-28.jpg
image.alt: A plate of Welsh rarebit on toasted bread

foods.text: A rich, mustard- and ale-spiked cheese sauce grilled onto toast, more elaborate than simple cheese on toast and a genuine national dish.
foods.whereToTry: Cafes and pubs throughout North Wales.

foods.name: Welsh lamb

image.file: File:A roast lamb Sunday dinner at Green Man pub, Takeley Street, Essex, England.jpg

foods.text: Grass-fed on the region's hills and mountains, Welsh lamb carries a protected geographical status and a strong reputation across Britain.
foods.whereToTry: Restaurants and pubs throughout the region, often as a Sunday roast.

foods.name: Bara brith
foods.text: A traditional fruit loaf soaked in tea and spiced, served sliced with butter, a genuine staple of Welsh tearooms.
foods.whereToTry: Tearooms and bakeries across North Wales.

foods.name: Welsh cakes
foods.text: Small, griddle-cooked fruited cakes, similar to a scone but flatter and denser, traditionally sold warm from the griddle at markets and cafes.
foods.whereToTry: Markets and cafes throughout Wales, often cooked fresh in front of you.

foods.name: Conwy mussels

image.alt: A bowl of freshly cooked mussels

foods.text: Conwy's estuary has produced mussels for centuries, and the town's harbour restaurants serve them fresh, often simply steamed with local ingredients.
foods.whereToTry: Harbourside restaurants in Conwy, particularly in the mussel season from September to March.

foods.name: Welsh ale and cider

image.file: File:Purple Moose Brewery Shop, Porthmadog - geograph.org.uk - 5511674.jpg
image.alt: The Purple Moose Brewery shop in Porthmadog, North Wales

foods.text: North Wales has a growing craft brewing scene alongside traditional cask ales, with several breweries producing distinctive local beers.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional pubs across the region, several serving beer from breweries within a short distance.

accommodation.intro: Llanberis and Betws-y-Coed are the two main mountain bases, with Conwy a good alternative for those prioritising the coast and castles.

areas.name: Llanberis
areas.bestFor: Climbing Snowdon and the slate landscape
areas.text: Sitting directly at the foot of Yr Wyddfa, the practical base for anyone prioritising the mountain and the railway.

areas.name: Betws-y-Coed
areas.bestFor: A central base for the wider park
areas.text: A picturesque village at the park's eastern edge, well placed for exploring the wider national park by car.

areas.name: Conwy
areas.text: A historic walled town on the coast, well placed for Conwy and Caernarfon Castles and day trips to Anglesey.

gettingThere.intro: Manchester and Liverpool are the nearest major airports, with a car useful once inside the region.

options.text: The most convenient major airport, roughly two hours by car to the heart of Snowdonia.
options.detail: Direct trains also run from Manchester to Bangor and Llandudno Junction, near the coast.

options.mode: Rail to Bangor or Llandudno Junction
options.text: Both stations sit on the North Wales coastal line, connecting to Chester, Manchester and Liverpool.
options.detail: Local buses and trains connect onward into the national park from either station.

options.text: The most flexible way to explore the wider region, particularly the Llŷn Peninsula and Anglesey.
options.detail: The A55 runs along the North Wales coast, providing quick access to Conwy, Bangor and Anglesey.

gettingAround.intro: A car is close to essential for covering the region's mountains and coastline together, though buses reach the main towns.

options.text: The most practical way to combine the mountains, castles and coastline in one trip.
options.detail: Mountain roads can be narrow and winding — allow more time than distances alone suggest.

options.text: A dedicated bus network connecting the main trailheads and villages around Yr Wyddfa, useful for point-to-point hikes.
options.detail: A practical way to start one trail and finish on a different one without needing to double back.

options.text: The Conwy Valley and Cambrian lines, alongside the narrow-gauge heritage railways, offer scenic and practical ways to move between towns.
options.detail: Timetables thin out considerably outside summer — check in advance for a shoulder-season visit.

bestTime.headline: May–June and September
bestTime.summary: Snowdonia's weather is changeable in any season, making daylight hours and crowd levels the more reliable planning factors.

seasons.text: Lengthening daylight, waterfalls at their fullest, and crowds well below the summer peak on the main trails.
The busiest months, with Yr Wyddfa's main paths and the Mountain Railway crowded, though the longest daylight for hiking.
Comfortable temperatures, thinning crowds, and often some of the year's clearest, most photogenic days on the mountains.
Wintry on the higher peaks, with snow and ice requiring proper equipment and experience for anything beyond the valleys.

bestTime.avoid: Bank holiday weekends in summer, when Yr Wyddfa's main car parks and paths become overcrowded.

itinerary.title: Four days in Snowdonia and North Wales
itinerary.intro: The mountain first, then castles and slate heritage, with a coastal day to close — a loop that covers the region's different sides.

days.title: Yr Wyddfa
days.morning: An early start up the Pyg Track or Llanberis Path, or the Mountain Railway for a less strenuous ascent.
days.afternoon: Continue the walk or descend, exploring Llanberis on return.

days.title: Slate heritage and Portmeirion
days.summary: The industry that shaped the region, and its most eccentric village.
days.morning: The National Slate Museum or a Blaenau Ffestiniog cavern tour.

days.title: Conwy and Caernarfon
days.summary: Two of Edward I's greatest castles.
days.morning: Conwy Castle and the town walls.
days.evening: Dinner by Conwy's harbour, with mussels if in season.

days.title: The Llŷn Peninsula or Anglesey
days.morning: Drive to Anglesey and South Stack's cliffs, or the Llŷn Peninsula's beaches.
days.afternoon: A coastal walk and a final Welsh cake stop.

tipsIntro: Practical notes on weather, booking and timing that make a real difference to a Snowdonia trip.
tips: Book the Snowdon Mountain Railway and slate cavern tours well ahead in summer — both sell out.
Check mountain-specific weather forecasts before any serious hike — conditions on Yr Wyddfa differ sharply from the valleys.
Start early for popular trailheads — Pen-y-Pass car park fills by mid-morning in summer.
Pack proper waterproofs and layers regardless of season — Snowdonia's weather changes fast.
Learn a few Welsh place-name pronunciations in advance — it's appreciated locally.
Combine Conwy and Caernarfon Castles with their town walls, both free and often overlooked in favour of the castles alone.
Allow more driving time than distances suggest — mountain roads are narrow and winding throughout the region.

faq.q: How many days do you need for Snowdonia and North Wales?
faq.a: Three to four. Three covers Yr Wyddfa and the main castles; four adds proper time for the coast or the slate heritage sites without feeling rushed.

faq.q: Do I need to be an experienced hiker to climb Snowdon?
faq.a: No — the Llanberis Path is a long but non-technical walk manageable by reasonably fit beginners, and the Mountain Railway offers a non-hiking alternative. The Pyg Track and Crib Goch are more serious and better suited to experienced walkers.

faq.q: What is the best time of year to visit?
faq.a: May to June and September offer the best balance of decent weather, long daylight and manageable crowds. Summer is busiest on the main trails; winter requires proper equipment and experience above the valleys.

Largely yes, particularly for combining the mountains with the coast. The Snowdon Sherpa bus network covers the main trailheads well, but the wider region, including Anglesey and the Llŷn Peninsula, is far easier with a car.

faq.q: Is Welsh widely spoken in this region?
faq.a: Yes — North Wales has some of the highest rates of Welsh as a first language in the country, and bilingual signage is standard throughout.
